transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-28
Time: 15:00 - 16:00 UTC
Duration: 60 minutes
Attendees: Daniel Park (Redwood AE), Sophie Martinez (Redwood SE), Ayesha Khan (Redwood SE), Rajesh Kumar (Aurelius - Platform Eng), Emily Ortiz (Aurelius - Security), Noah Fisher (Aurelius - ML Infra), Laura Chen (Aurelius - CTO)

Summary (auto):
High-level technical deep dive on Private VPC deployment. Focus on networking (PrivateLink, NAT, subnets, routing), runtime considerations for latency and throughput (batching, KV cache, quantization), and a plan to run in-VPC benchmarks. Action items assigned for network details, diagrams, and benchmark setup.

Topics: PrivateLink setup, VPC peering vs PrivateLink, NAT/gateway patterns, DNS resolution for PrivateLink endpoints, cross-AZ connectivity, egress/bastion patterns, runtime batching and KV cache behavior over network, quantization tradeoffs for latency, benchmarking plan.

Transcript:
[00:00] Daniel Park: Hey everyone thanks for joining, we'll keep this technical and focused. We've got about an hour, and Sophie and Ayesha will lead through networking and runtime impacts.
[00:12] Laura Chen: Great, thanks. We want to understand what it looks like to run Redwood Private in our VPC; security, perf, and how networking affects latency are the big ones.
[00:20] Sophie Martinez: Perfect. Quick agenda: PrivateLink architecture, DNS and route considerations, NAT and egress, then runtime effects - batching, KV cache, quantization. We'll finish with next steps and a benchmark plan.
[00:33] Rajesh Kumar: For context, our infra is in us-east-1 across three AZs. We have k8s clusters for inference jobs, and we prefer no public internet egress for inference traffic. We also use Transit Gateway in some accounts.
[00:47] Emily Ortiz: From security: SOC2, encryption at rest and in transit, and KMS integration are must-haves. We'll need audit logs.
[00:55] Sophie Martinez: Understood. For Private deployments we support a PrivateLink endpoint that lives in your VPC — it's a customer-facing interface to Redwood's control plane or data plane depending on the architecture you choose. A note: sometimes transcripts say PrivateLink incorrectly as Private Link or Private-L; I might say Private-L a few times, sorry.
[01:12] Noah Fisher: Quick Q: do you require cross-account VPC peering or is PrivateLink enough? We want to avoid peering if possible because of routing complexity.
[01:20] Ayesha Khan: PrivateLink is our recommended approach for most customers. It avoids routing table explosion and gives you an endpoint network interface (ENI) in your subnet. You don't need peering. The PrivateLink endpoint can be associated with multiple subnets across AZs for HA.
[01:36] Rajesh Kumar: How about DNS? We run internal DNS and split-horizon. Will the PrivateLink require us to override DNS names?
[01:44] Sophie Martinez: Good question. We publish a private DNS name that you can enable in the VPC; when enabled it resolves to the endpoint ENIs. If you have split-horizon DNS, you'll want to add a conditional forward or an override — many customers add a Route53 private hosted zone or configure their internal resolver to forward the redwood domain to the VPC resolver.
[01:58] Emily Ortiz: That hits our internal workflows. Also curious about certificate validation — TLS with mutual TLS?
[02:05] Sophie Martinez: We use mTLS for control-plane traffic in Private deployments; for data-plane inference traffic we support TLS with client certs and optional mTLS depending on the contract. We can integrate with your KMS for keys. We'll share the exact TLS cert rotation and PKI docs.
[02:21] Laura Chen: Excellent. Now from a perf side what are the main network-induced latency costs we should expect?
[02:28] Ayesha Khan: Network adds two areas: control-plane RPCs (model load, health checks) and data-plane token streaming. For PrivateLink the additional hop is minimal inside the AZ but cross-AZ ENI hairpins can add 1-5 ms depending on AZ pairing and route table setup.
[02:44] Noah Fisher: If the inference runtime lives outside our VPC (i.e., hosted), obviously egress goes over the internet or through a NAT; with Private the data plane is in our VPC so that should be better, right?
[02:55] Sophie Martinez: Correct. With Redwood Private running in your VPC (we bring the runtime), the per-token latency is dominated by the runtime's model forward pass and the KM/kv cache lookups. If you run the runtime in a separate subnet in the same AZ and keep ENIs local, network overhead is small. If the request crosses AZs or uses NAT gateway egress, you'll see higher tail latency.
[03:13] Rajesh Kumar: We have a policy of keeping workloads in private subnets with no public IPs. How do we manage outbound traffic for things like model pulls, telemetry, or updates?
[03:22] Sophie Martinez: Options: managed NAT gateway, NAT instances, or VPC endpoints for S3/ecr for model pulls. For telemetry/control-plane you can use PrivateLink endpoints to Redwood's control-plane or a proxied egress configuration. Many customers use S3 VPC endpoints for model artifacts and avoid NAT entirely for model pulls.
[03:39] Daniel Park: One common pattern is to put the inference nodes in private subnets with route to S3 via VPC endpoints and use PrivateLink for control signals. That keeps egress minimal.
[03:48] Noah Fisher: About KV cache — if the KV cache is sharded and lives on separate hosts, how sensitive is it to network latency? We care about per-token tail p99s.
[03:56] Ayesha Khan: KV cache is latency-sensitive. In our runtime the KV cache is typically local to the GPU host (shared memory or fast local NVMe). If you configure multi-host KV (for very large models or multi-host sharding), cross-host RPCs can add ms of latency per cache miss. We recommend co-locating KV cache shards with the model replicas and keeping those in the same AZ to reduce p95/p99.
[04:17] Rajesh Kumar: If we can't avoid cross-AZ for capacity, what mitigations do you recommend?
[04:22] Sophie Martinez: Two main mitigations: 1) tune batching so that more tokens are amortized per network roundtrip, and 2) use async prefetching/prefix cache to warm the KV cache. Also consider quantization — smaller model weights mean faster kernel exec and lower token times, which can hide some network latency. But quantization trades accuracy for speed.
[04:40] Emily Ortiz: On quantization — what levels are supported and do you have metrics on quality regressions? We need to know expected degradation for our NLU tasks.
[04:48] Sophie Martinez: We support 8-bit and 4-bit quantization profiles, and we have Redwood Optimize recommendations per workload. We'll share evaluation reports. For most instruction-following LLMs 8-bit has near-zero quality impact; 4-bit sometimes shows small regressions on edge cases. We'll run a small eval on your prompts as part of the POC.
[05:05] Noah Fisher: Batching: if we increase batch size, does that increase latency for single requests? We have low-latency endpoints that need sub-50ms tail ideally.
[05:12] Ayesha Khan: There's a trade-off. Batching increases throughput and reduces cost per token but adds queuing latency. We have dynamic batching policies (latency SLO-based) where the system will flush a batch based on time or size thresholds. For sub-50ms tail you typically run smaller batches, possibly single-request fast-paths on dedicated hardware. We'll show config knobs.
[05:30] Rajesh Kumar: About NAT: we prefer to avoid NAT gateways to save cost, but our compliance team wants auditability and limited egress. Any patterns?
[05:38] Daniel Park: Some customers use egress via a centralized restricted account with Transit Gateway and a managed NAT fleet that logs via VPC flow logs and proxy. Alternatively, use VPC Interface endpoints (for S3, ECR) to remove egress. PrivateLink for control-plane helps remove most public egress.
[05:53] Emily Ortiz: We also require long-term audit logs for inference requests metadata (not content). Can Redwood stream or push logs into our SIEM?
[06:00] Sophie Martinez: Yes, we can integrate with your audit pipeline. We can push operational logs to Kinesis/CloudWatch or S3 buckets via VPC endpoints. We'll map fields and ensure PII is excluded from logs per your policy.
[06:12] Laura Chen: Can you walk through a sample networking diagram? Like subnets, endpoint placement, and routing rules?
[06:20] Ayesha Khan: Sure — (Sophie shares screen - noted link: https://redwood-internal.example.com/diagrams/aurelius-privatelink — link shared in notes). Typical layout: 3 private subnets (one per AZ) for inference pods, PrivateLink ENIs in those subnets, S3 and ECR VPC endpoints in same subnets, optional NAT gateway in a centralized infra account for limited egress, and security groups that allow only specific ports to the runtime.
[06:43] Rajesh Kumar: If we use Transit Gateway, anything special?
[06:47] Sophie Martinez: With Transit Gateway make sure the route propagation sends traffic to the correct subnets. PrivateLink still works across TGW attachments if the endpoint ENIs are reachable. Some customers attach the PrivateLink endpoints to an account and then use TGW routing; test for asymmetric routing.
[06:59] Noah Fisher: On model pull performance: we have large model artifacts (~20-50GB). If we use S3 VPC endpoints, how long to pull and what's impact on startup time?
[07:08] Ayesha Khan: Pull time depends on instance network bandwidth. With enhanced networking in AWS and multithreaded downloads, a 50GB model can pull in ~1-3 minutes on an instance with >=10 Gbps. To reduce cold-starts we recommend warm pools and image-based runtime caching or EBS snapshots preloaded.
[07:25] Emily Ortiz: Any constraints around cross-account roles for PrivateLink?
[07:29] Sophie Martinez: You'll need to allow the AWS endpoint service and accept an endpoint connection if we use AWS PrivateLink across accounts. We provide CloudFormation/Terraform to automate the handshake and policy.
[07:39] Daniel Park: Switching to runtime specifics: how does KV cache eviction and rehydration behave under network flakiness?
[07:45] Ayesha Khan: Good question. Our runtime persists KV cache locally and asynchronously writes checkpoints to local NVMe. If a host restarts, we can warm from disk or from a peer. In high flakiness scenarios we recommend more aggressive replication or using larger batch sizes to reduce dependency on immediate cache hits.
[08:03] Noah Fisher: For throughput testing, what metrics should we capture?
[08:07] Sophie Martinez: Capture per-request latency (p50/p95/p99), tokens-per-second, GPU utilization, KV cache hit rate, network RTT, retransmits, and model load time. We'll provide a benchmark harness to automate this.
[08:20] Rajesh Kumar: For the in-VPC benchmark, do you need privileged access to our cluster or will you run an external workload that talks over PrivateLink?
[08:28] Sophie Martinez: We can do both. Option A: we run a container in your cluster (via a temporary service account) to generate realistic traffic — this gives best fidelity. Option B: run from a Redwood-managed test agent wired via PrivateLink — less intrusive but slightly different network path. We'll coordinate with Noah on preferred option.
[08:45] Emily Ortiz: Time sync and clock skew can affect logs; please note we need consistent timestamps.
[08:50] Ayesha Khan: We'll coordinate NTP/chrony recommendations and include timestamp normalization in the log pipeline.
[08:58] Laura Chen: Any gotchas with DNS TTL causing stale ENI resolution during endpoint failover?
[09:04] Sophie Martinez: Yes — if you enable private DNS, Route53 resolver caches can hold old ENI IPs until TTL expires. We advise low TTLs on the redwood domain and use health-check-driven endpoint failover; our SDK also retries on connection failures.
[09:20] Noah Fisher: How do we handle versioned model rollouts in this architecture? Canary traffic needs to hit different model variants without leaking data.
[09:27] Daniel Park: Redwood's deployment supports per-route model pins and canary policies. You can configure routing policies at the edge or in the control plane; with Private deployments the routing control plane can be on-prem or in your VPC and we'll honor A/B splits. We'll also support tagging requests for audit separation.
[09:45] Rajesh Kumar: Anything else we should consider for resiliency?
[09:49] Ayesha Khan: Multi-AZ placement, health checks at the LB level, circuit breakers that fallback to a lower-cost model variant, and pre-warmed capacity. Also, ensure your security groups allow cross-AZ traffic for the inference subnets.
[10:03] Emily Ortiz: Action items recap?
[10:06] Daniel Park: Sophie can you recap?
[10:08] Sophie Martinez: Sure — we'll provide: PrivateLink diagram + Terraform snippets, DNS recommendations and example Route53 zone config, quantization eval run on sample prompts, benchmark harness and suggested metrics, and our SOC2/KMS docs. Rajesh will send VPC/subnet CIDRs and indicate NAT preference. Noah will share traffic profiles. Daniel will send initial pricing options and timeline.
[10:30] Laura Chen: Sounds good. We'll review and get back with the network info by end of week.
[10:36] Daniel Park: Thanks all. We'll follow up in email with links and the action items.
